procedural_history.originating_court: Additional Sessions Judge, Special Judge, Lucknow (‘trial court’)
procedural_history.impugned_order: Order dated 03.04.2023 passed by the High Court of Judicature at Allahabad, Lucknow Bench in Criminal Miscellaneous Bail Application No. 2282 of 2021 (Sheikh Javed Iqbal @ Ashfaq Ansari @ Javed Ansari Vs. State of U.P.) denying bail to the appellant.
procedural_history.high_court_proceedings:
1. Appellant filed an application before the High Court under Section 482 of Cr.P.C. for quashing of the trial court's order dated 27.05.2016 rejecting his discharge application and the order dated 16.07.2016 framing charges against him.
2. Appellant filed a bail application before the High Court which was dismissed by the impugned order dated 03.04.2023.
procedural_history.supreme_court_posture:
1. State of U.P. assailed the order of the High Court dated 08.10.2021 before this Court by filing Special Leave to Appeal (Criminal) No. 861 of 2022. This Court by order dated 11.02.2022 issued notice and in the meanwhile directed stay of the order of the High Court dated 08.10.2021.
2. The appellant approached the Supreme Court challenging the High Court's order dated 03.04.2023 denying him bail by filing Special Leave Petition (Criminal) Diary No. 11387 of 2024, which was later registered as Special Leave Petition (Criminal) No. 5260 of 2024 after the delay was condoned. The Supreme Court heard the matter and disposed of the appeal, setting aside the High Court's order.

directions: The impugned order dated 03.04.2023 of the High Court is set aside and quashed;

issue.issue_text: Whether the High Court was correct in dismissing the appellant's application under Section 482 of the Cr.P.C. for quashing the trial court's orders, which had rejected the discharge application and framed charges against the appellant.

facts: The appellant filed an application under Section 482 of the Cr.P.C. before the High Court.
The application sought to quash two orders from the trial court: one rejecting the appellant's discharge application and another framing charges against him under the IPC and the UAP Act.
law: The High Court examined the validity of the sanction required for prosecution under the Unlawful Activities (Prevention) Act (UAP Act).
Under Section 45(2) of the UAP Act, a valid sanction for prosecution must be based on a recommendation made after an independent review of the evidence collected during the investigation.
application: The High Court found that the sanction to prosecute the appellant for the offence under Section 16 of the UAP Act was not based on the mandatory independent review of evidence.
It concluded that this failure amounted to a "clear case of non-application of mind" by the State, rendering the sanction orders invalid.
reasoning.conclusion: Due to the invalid sanction, the High Court held that the trial court was barred from taking cognizance of the offence under Section 16 of the UAP Act. Consequently, it partially allowed the appellant's application by quashing the trial court's orders and the charge to the extent of the UAP Act offence. The High Court directed the trial to proceed only for the remaining offences under Sections 489B and 489C of the IPC.

arguments.issue_text: Whether the High Court was correct in dismissing the appellant's application under Section 482 of the Cr.P.C. for quashing the trial court's orders, which had rejected the discharge application and framed charges against the appellant.

cases.case_name: Union of India v. K.A. Najeeb
cases.principle: The right to life and personal liberty under Article 21 is overarching, allowing a constitutional court to grant bail to an accused despite restrictive statutory provisions in a penal statute if it finds that the accused's rights have been infringed, for instance, by prolonged incarceration.

cases.case_name: Javed Gulam Nabi Shaikh v. State of Maharashtra
cases.principle: The right to life and personal liberty under Article 21 is overarching, allowing a constitutional court to grant bail to an accused despite restrictive statutory provisions in a penal statute if it finds that the accused's rights have been infringed.

ratio_decidendi.ratio: A constitutional court is not restrained from granting bail to an accused on account of restrictive statutory provisions in a penal statute if it finds that the undertrial's right to life and personal liberty under Article 21 of the Constitution has been infringed. In such an event, the statutory restrictions on bail will not stand in the way, as the constitutional right is overarching and sacrosanct.
obiter: The over-arching postulate of criminal jurisprudence that an accused is presumed to be innocent until proven guilty cannot be brushed aside lightly, howsoever stringent the penal law may be.

Even in the case of interpretation of a penal statute, howsoever stringent it may be, a constitutional court has to lean in favour of constitutionalism and the rule of law of which liberty is an intrinsic part.

judicial_reasoning.core_finding: The appellant's continued incarceration is unjustified because the manner in which the prosecuting agency and the Court have proceeded has infringed the accused's right to a speedy trial, thereby violating Article 21 of the Constitution. The right to life and personal liberty under Article 21 is overarching and sacrosanct, and a constitutional court cannot be restrained from granting bail by restrictive statutory provisions in a penal statute if it finds that this fundamental right has been infringed.
legal_tests_applied: Balancing of competing interests: The court must balance the liberty of a citizen against the interest of the victims and the collective interest of the community. The ultimate justification for deprivation of liberty of an undertrial can only be on account of the accused-undertrial being found guilty, and if such a finding is not likely to be arrived at within a reasonable time, some relief becomes necessary.

Infringement of Article 21: A constitutional court must determine if the right of the accused-undertrial under Article 21 has been infringed, particularly due to the length of the period spent in custody and the unlikelihood of the trial being completed soon. If such an infringement is found, restrictive statutory provisions on bail would not come in the way of granting relief.
why_respondent_won: The court acknowledged the respondent's position regarding the seriousness of the case, stating: "we are conscious of the fact that the charges levelled against the respondent are grave and a serious threat to societal harmony. Had it been a case at the threshold, we would have outrightly turned down the respondent’s prayer."
policy_considerations: The right to life and personal liberty enshrined under Article 21 of the Constitution of India is overarching and sacrosanct.

Even in the case of interpretation of a penal statute, howsoever stringent it may be, a constitutional court has to lean in favour of constitutionalism and the rule of law of which liberty is an intrinsic part.
It would be very wrong to say that under a particular statute, bail cannot be granted. It would run counter to the very grain of our constitutional jurisprudence.
